note: Faithful rule manifest for the mechanics of release/CI-gate/rollback/artifact-integrity/backup/irreversible-action-confirmation operations, distilled from SemVer 2.0.0, Keep a Changelog 1.1.0, and the official GitHub Actions documentation. The .md is authoritative and unchanged; this indexes every actionable rule, typed checkable|judgment|principle, with predicate/reviewer_criterion. This module deliberately does not duplicate engineering-leadership's §5 (versioning/changelog ownership) or git-mastery's tag/signing mechanics — those are cross-referenced, not repeated. Rules tagged [INFERRED] in the guide carry no single primary source and are labeled accordingly, matching the evidence discipline of the other shipped expertise modules. COMPLETE — all of §0–§10 + Defaults table + Source ledger captured in som-1..som-46 (guide authored and read in full; no content dropped). sections_accounted maps every section to its rules.

rules.text: Read this guide as the mechanical layer beneath three ownership decisions engineering-leadership already covers: what a version number promises, what a changelog entry says, and when a release is trustworthy enough to ship. This guide is 'how the promise is executed' — the exact SemVer precedence algorithm, the exact changelog markers for a pulled release, the exact CI wiring that turns a gate into something that actually blocks a merge, the exact command sequence a release and a rollback run, and the exact confirmation an irreversible action requires before it runs.

The single rule threaded through every section: never run an irreversible or outward-facing action — deploy, publish/release, push or force-push, delete — without the user's explicit authorization, and always present the exact command plus its blast radius when asking (§8). Release mechanics, rollback mechanics, and artifact integrity all exist to make that one confirmed action as safe and reversible as possible once authorized.

A gate — a required status check, a branch-protection rule, a needs dependency, a lint threshold — exists to be satisfied by fixing the underlying problem, never by weakening the gate itself; a red main blocks every release. Mirrors engineering-leadership's stance on technical debt (lead-43), applied here at the CI-pipeline layer (§3, som-18).

A normal version number MUST take the form X.Y.Z where X, Y, Z are non-negative integers with no leading zeroes, and each element MUST increase numerically — e.g. 1.9.0 → 1.10.0 → 1.11.0 (numeric, not lexical, ordering). [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 2]

predicate.spec: a version string matches ^(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*)\.(0|[1-9]\d*) (no leading zeroes on any component) and each successive release's major/minor/patch compares strictly greater numerically, never by lexical string ordering.

rules.text: A pre-release version is denoted by a hyphen plus dot-separated ASCII alphanumeric/hyphen identifiers immediately after the patch version; identifiers MUST NOT be empty and a purely-numeric identifier MUST NOT have leading zeroes. A pre-release version always has lower precedence than its associated normal version. Examples: 1.0.0-alpha, 1.0.0-alpha.1, 1.0.0-0.3.7, 1.0.0-x.7.z.92, 1.0.0-x-y-z.--. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 9]

predicate.spec: a pre-release suffix (after the first unescaped hyphen following patch) consists only of non-empty dot-separated [0-9A-Za-z-] identifiers with no numeric identifier carrying a leading zero, and any pre-release version X.Y.Z-<id> compares as lower precedence than the plain X.Y.Z.

rules.text: Build metadata is denoted by a plus sign plus dot-separated identifiers after the patch or pre-release version (same character rules as pre-release). Build metadata MUST be ignored when determining precedence — two versions differing only in build metadata have identical precedence. Examples: 1.0.0-alpha+001, 1.0.0+20130313144700, 1.0.0-beta+exp.sha.5114f85. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 10]

predicate.spec: any version-comparison/precedence logic strips a +<build> suffix before comparing, so two version strings identical except for build metadata are treated as equal precedence, and no deploy/promotion decision keys off build-metadata content alone.

rules.text: The full precedence algorithm: (1) split into major/minor/patch/pre-release, build metadata never enters; (2) compare major, minor, patch numerically, first difference wins — 1.0.0 < 2.0.0 < 2.1.0 < 2.1.1; (3) if equal, a pre-release version has lower precedence than the normal version — 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0; (4) if both pre-release with equal major.minor.patch, compare dot-separated identifiers left-to-right until a difference: numeric-only identifiers compare numerically, alphanumeric/hyphenated identifiers compare lexically in ASCII sort order, a numeric identifier always has lower precedence than a non-numeric one, and if every earlier identifier is equal a larger set of fields outranks a smaller set. Full chain: 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0-alpha.1 < 1.0.0-alpha.beta < 1.0.0-beta < 1.0.0-beta.2 < 1.0.0-beta.11 < 1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0. [VERIFIED, semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html, item 11, full text confirmed via raw fetched page]

predicate.spec: a version-precedence comparator implements exactly this ordered algorithm (numeric major.minor.patch first, then pre-release-vs-normal, then per-identifier comparison with numeric<non-numeric and larger-set-wins-on-tie) and reproduces the worked example chain 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0-alpha.1 < 1.0.0-alpha.beta < 1.0.0-beta < 1.0.0-beta.2 < 1.0.0-beta.11 < 1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0.

rules.text: Use a pre-release identifier as the mechanical gate for a staged rollout — tag a candidate 2.0.0-rc.1, run it through the real release pipeline (§4), and promote by cutting the plain 2.0.0 tag once verified, never by mutating the rc tag's target in place (cross-ref engineering-leadership lead-34 and git-mastery git-9/git-59 for the tag-object mechanics).
rules.reviewer_criterion: Did a staged rollout use a genuinely new, higher-precedence pre-release/release tag at each promotion step, rather than moving an existing tag's target to point at different content?

rules.text: Mark a release that had to be pulled for a serious bug or security issue with a loud, structured [YANKED] tag on its own heading — '## [0.0.5] - 2014-12-13 [YANKED]' — rather than quietly deleting or omitting that version's entry. [VERIFIED verbatim marker, keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ — "What about yanked releases?"]

predicate.spec: a changelog entry for a pulled/withdrawn release carries a bracketed [YANKED] tag on its version heading (e.g. matches /\[YANKED\]\s*$/ on the '## [X.Y.Z] - date' line) rather than being deleted or silently omitted.

rules.text: Treat the Yanked marker as the changelog's half of a rollback: it must be paired with the actual operational act — redeploying the last good build (§5) or shipping an immediate patch release — not left standing alone as a documentation-only edit. [INFERRED — direct extension of the Yanked mechanic]

predicate.spec: a commit/PR that adds a [YANKED] marker to the changelog is accompanied (same change or a directly linked follow-up) by either a rollback deployment or a new patch release fixing the yanked version's defect.

rules.text: Do not rely on a platform's native release notes (e.g. GitHub Releases) as the sole system of record for changelog history — such release pages are non-portable, historically less discoverable than a repository-root file, and offered no built-in links to the commit/diff log between releases. Prefer a plain, portable CHANGELOG.md as the primary artifact; a platform release page may mirror it, but should not replace it. [VERIFIED, keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/ — "What about GitHub Releases?"]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Does a portable CHANGELOG.md (or equivalent versioned file) exist as the actual system of record, with any platform release page treated as, at most, a mirror of it?

rules.text: Protect the integration branch with a branch protection rule requiring specific status checks before a merge is allowed, and keep job names unique across every workflow in the repository — reusing a job name in two workflow files can produce ambiguous or duplicated status-check results that block a PR even when the real checks passed. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/repositories/.../about-protected-branches — "About branch protection rules" tip]

predicate.spec: the default/integration branch has a branch-protection rule with required status checks configured, and no two workflow files in the repository define a job with the same job name/id.

rules.text: By default, a branch protection rule's restrictions do not apply to users with admin permissions. Decide explicitly whether admins are bound by the same required checks as everyone else, rather than leaving this permissive default unexamined. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/repositories/.../about-protected-branches — "Do not allow bypassing the above settings"]

predicate.spec: the branch-protection configuration's admin-bypass setting was reviewed and set intentionally (documented as on or off), not left at the tool's unexamined default.

rules.text: Sequence dependent CI jobs with jobs.<job_id>.needs: a job runs only once every job it needs has completed successfully. If a needed job fails or is skipped, every job depending on it — transitively down the dependency chain — is skipped too, unless that job's if: explicitly uses always() to opt back in. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax — jobs.<job_id>.needs]

predicate.spec: a gated downstream job (deploy/release/publish) declares jobs.<job_id>.needs naming every upstream check job it depends on, and does not use an unconditional always() that would let it run after an upstream failure/skip.

rules.text: Scope the CI token to least privilege explicitly, rather than leaving the default broad scope implicit: set permissions: at the workflow level (e.g. permissions: read-all) or per job (e.g. permissions: {issues: write, pull-requests: write}, granting exactly those scopes and no access to anything unlisted). A workflow that never declares permissions: is trusting whatever the repository/org default happens to be. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../workflow-syntax — permissions and jobs.<job_id>.permissions]

predicate.spec: every workflow file declares an explicit permissions: block (workflow-level and/or per-job) rather than relying on the repository/organization default token scope.

rules.text: When one workflow calls another (a reusable workflow), secrets do not cross that boundary implicitly — use jobs.<job_id>.secrets.inherit to deliberately pass all of the calling workflow's accessible secrets (organization, repository, environment) into the called workflow, including across repositories/organizations. Treat this as a scoping decision made on purpose, not a default. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../workflow-syntax — jobs.<job_id>.secrets.inherit]

predicate.spec: a reusable-workflow call either passes named secrets explicitly or uses secrets: inherit as a deliberate, reviewed choice — never silently assumes secrets are available in the called workflow without one of these being present.

rules.text: Prevent overlapping or racing runs with concurrency: group runs under a key (e.g. ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}) and set cancel-in-progress deliberately. GitHub Actions' default with no concurrency block is to allow multiple (uncapped by default) concurrent runs/jobs — true auto-cancels a superseded in-progress run, false lets an already-running job finish undisturbed. Concurrency-group names must be unique across workflows or an unrelated workflow's run can be cancelled by mistake. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../workflow-syntax — concurrency, "default behavior... allow multiple jobs or workflow runs to run concurrently"]

predicate.spec: a deploy or release workflow declares a concurrency: {group, cancel-in-progress} block with a group key unique to that workflow/environment, rather than relying on the uncapped-by-default multiple-concurrent-runs default.

rules.text: Never weaken or skip a required check, a branch-protection rule, or a needs gate to get a red build merged — fix the underlying failure, or change the check itself through the same review process as any other code change, never as a side effect of getting unblocked (som-3). [INFERRED — house convention, mirrors lead-43's stance for a lint rule or test]

predicate.spec: no commit disables, loosens, or bypasses a required status check, branch-protection rule, or jobs.needs gate as the mechanism for getting a failing change merged; the change that touches a gate's definition goes through the same review as any other code change.

rules.text: Reference a GitHub Actions environment (e.g. production) from a deploying job. Every protection rule configured for that environment must pass before the job is even dispatched to a runner; the job can read the environment's secrets only after it has been sent to a runner. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/deployment-environments]

predicate.spec: a deploying job declares environment: <name>, and any secrets it consumes are environment-scoped secrets available only once that environment's protection rules have passed and the job has been dispatched.

rules.text: Configure environment protection mechanically as up to three independent controls: required reviewers (up to 6 people/teams, only one approval needed, optional 'Prevent self-review'), a wait timer (fixed minutes to hold), and deployment branch policies restricting which branches/tags may deploy. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments — "Creating an environment"]

predicate.spec: a production-grade environment has at least one of {required reviewers, wait timer, deployment branch policy} explicitly configured, with required-reviewer approval count and self-review policy set intentionally rather than left at defaults.

rules.text: Decide explicitly whether administrators may bypass an environment's configured protection rules — leaving this enabled by default silently creates a path around every required-reviewer and wait-timer gate just configured for that environment (the environment-level twin of som-13). [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments]

predicate.spec: the environment's admin-bypass-protection-rules setting was reviewed and set intentionally, not left at the tool's unexamined default.

rules.text: Gate a release or rollback trigger behind workflow_dispatch with typed inputs (received via the inputs context; up to 25 top-level input properties, 65,535-character total payload) whenever the action must be a deliberate, on-demand human act rather than an automatic reaction to a push. This is the CI-pipeline's mechanical form of the §8 confirmation gate. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../workflow-syntax — on.workflow_dispatch and on.workflow_dispatch.inputs]

predicate.spec: a release/rollback workflow is triggered by on.workflow_dispatch with named, typed inputs (not solely an automatic push/schedule trigger), making the run a deliberate manually-invoked act.

rules.text: Tag every release with an annotated (and, where the project requires provenance, signed) tag — never a lightweight one. This module does not re-derive the git object-model reason (only an annotated tag is a real tag object a release tool can attach notes to, and only an annotated tag can carry a GPG signature); that mechanic belongs to git-mastery (git-9, git-58-git-60) and is cross-referenced here, not repeated.

Prefer roll-forward (ship a new, higher-precedence version fixing the regression) over any notion of 'rolling back a release number' as the default recovery path — a published version's contents are immutable once released, so there is no operation that un-publishes 1.2.3; 'rolling back' always means redeploying a prior, still-intact artifact while the broken version stays visible in history (Yanked per som-9), never rewriting or removing the broken version's record.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Did the recovery either ship a new, higher version, or redeploy a specific prior artifact by reference — rather than attempting to edit, delete, or renumber the already-published broken version?

rules.text: A deployment rollback is 'redeploy the last-known-good build artifact,' not 'reset the version number backward.' Version numbers and currently-deployed state are two independent axes; keep the previous version's build artifact retrievable specifically so this redeploy is always possible on short notice — this is why artifact integrity/retention (§6) and backup discipline (§7) are prerequisites to a usable rollback, not optional extras.

predicate.spec: the documented/executed rollback procedure redeploys a retained prior build artifact by reference (tag, digest, or archive) rather than attempting to decrement or otherwise mutate the current version number.

rules.text: When the failing behavior sits behind a feature flag or config toggle, prefer flipping the flag off over running a full artifact rollback — a flag flip is near-instant and needs no re-run of the deploy pipeline, whereas a full rollback re-triggers every gate in §3-§4. Reserve full artifact rollback for regressions not isolated behind a flag. [INFERRED — standard progressive-delivery practice]
rules.reviewer_criterion: For a regression isolated behind a flag/toggle, was the flag flipped off before (or instead of) triggering a full deployment rollback?

rules.text: Establish build provenance for a release artifact with a GitHub Actions attestation: grant the building job three permissions — id-token (write), contents (read, not write), and attestations (write) — adding packages (write) only for a container image, then run actions/attest@v4 after the build step — a subject-path input for a binary, or a subject-name (fully-qualified image name, no tag) plus a subject-digest input (the artifact's own content digest) for a container image. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/use-artifact-attestations/use-artifact-attestations — "Generating build provenance for binaries" and "Generating build provenance for container images"]

predicate.spec: the release-build job's permissions block sets id-token to write, contents to read (not write), and attestations to write (plus packages to write for a container image), and includes an actions/attest@v4 step after the build step with subject-path or subject-name+subject-digest set.

rules.text: Verify, not just generate, an artifact's attestation before trusting it: use the GitHub CLI attestation-verify command against the artifact path (or, after a registry login, against the oci:// reference for a container image). Generation without a consumer-side verification step proves nothing was checked. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../use-artifact-attestations — "Verifying artifact attestations with the GitHub CLI"]

predicate.spec: consuming/deploying a released artifact is preceded by a gh attestation verify (or equivalent) step against that artifact, not merely by trusting that a build attestation was generated at some point.

rules.text: Attach a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) attestation alongside the build attestation via the same actions/attest@v4 action's SBOM-path input, and verify it by naming its predicate type explicitly (an SPDX or CycloneDX document reference). A build attestation proves who built it and how; an SBOM attestation additionally proves what went into it. [VERIFIED, docs.github.com/.../use-artifact-attestations — "Generating an attestation for a software bill of materials (SBOM)" and "Verifying an attestation for SBOMs"]

predicate.spec: a build/release pipeline that produces a build attestation also produces a paired SBOM attestation for the same artifact, and SBOM verification names an explicit predicate type rather than relying on the default predicate.

rules.text: For an artifact distributed outside GitHub's attestation feature (e.g. a plain tarball on another host), publish, at minimum, a checksum manifest alongside the artifact, plus a detached cryptographic signature over that checksum manifest against a key the consumer can actually verify — write-time integrity, not an after-the-fact promise. [INFERRED — standard practitioner convention paralleling the GitHub-native attestation mechanism]

predicate.spec: any release artifact distributed outside a platform-native attestation mechanism ships with a checksum manifest file and a detached signature over that manifest, verifiable against a published key.

rules.text: Back up a durable datastore on a schedule matched to its actual write rate and the project's tolerance for data loss (its Recovery Point Objective), and keep at least one copy off the primary host/region. A backup stored only alongside the data it protects is not a defense against disk failure, region loss, or an accidental delete of the whole volume. [INFERRED — standard operational convention]

predicate.spec: a durable datastore has a scheduled backup process whose cadence is documented against an explicit RPO, and at least one backup copy is stored off the primary host/region from the live data.

rules.text: A backup that has never been restored is unverified. Schedule and actually run periodic restore drills into an isolated environment; a backup job that exits 0 but was never test-restored is an unproven claim of safety, not a working one. [INFERRED — standard operational convention]

predicate.spec: periodic restore drills into an isolated environment are scheduled and their execution/results are recorded, not merely inferred from the backup job's exit code.

rules.text: For a structured or bi-temporal datastore (cross-ref memory-management §5/§9 for one concrete instance), a restore or import step must re-validate internal consistency — structural invariants, foreign-key/reference integrity, duplicate detection — rather than trusting the restored bytes blindly. A corrupted or partially-written backup can restore 'successfully' while still being silently wrong. [INFERRED — direct extension of standard restore-verification practice]

predicate.spec: a restore/import routine for a structured datastore runs an explicit consistency/integrity check (schema validation, referential-integrity check, or equivalent) after loading the backup, before the restored store is treated as trustworthy.

rules.text: Treat a destructive migration or schema change against a live datastore as the same class of irreversible action as a delete (§8): take a fresh, verified backup immediately beforehand, and confirm the rollback path (a restore point, or a working down-migration) actually functions before running the forward migration in production.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Before a destructive live-datastore migration ran, did a verified-fresh backup exist and was the rollback/down-migration path confirmed working, rather than assumed?

rules.text: Never run an irreversible or outward-facing action — a deploy, a publish/release, a git push (or force-push), or a delete — without the user's explicit authorization. Build, test, lint, dry-run, read operations, and uncommitted local edits are exempt and flow freely (som-38); this gate exists specifically for the class of action that leaves the local, reversible working copy and either cannot be cheaply undone or becomes visible/consumable to a party outside that local workspace.

predicate.spec: before executing a deploy, a publish/release, a git push or force-push, or a delete against any datastore/environment outside the local uncommitted workspace, the agent has obtained the user's explicit, affirmative authorization for that specific action in the current turn; build/test/lint/dry-run/read/local-uncommitted-edit operations are not gated by this check.

rules.text: When requesting that authorization, present the exact command that will run and its blast radius — what changes, who or what is affected, and whether the action is itself reversible — before executing anything. A vague 'should I proceed?' with no concrete command and no stated consequence is not a real confirmation request.

predicate.spec: the authorization request presented to the user includes the literal command/action to be executed and an explicit statement of its blast radius (scope of change, affected parties/systems, reversibility) rather than a generic yes/no prompt with no specifics.

rules.text: Silence is not consent. If the user does not explicitly respond to a presented irreversible/outward-facing action, do not proceed on the assumption that 'no objection means go' — re-ask, or stop and wait.

predicate.spec: an irreversible/outward-facing action is executed only after an explicit affirmative response from the user in the conversation; the absence of any response is treated as non-consent, not as approval.

rules.text: Build, test, lint, dry-run, and read operations, and any edit that stays uncommitted in the local working copy, are explicitly exempt from this gate and should flow without a confirmation step — the gate exists for irreversible/outward-facing actions specifically, not as a blanket brake on every command. Applying it indiscriminately trains asking-and-being-ignored, the failure mode som-3/som-18 warn against for gates in general.

predicate.spec: build, test, lint, dry-run, read, and local-uncommitted-edit operations execute without requiring the som-35 authorization step; the confirmation gate is scoped only to the irreversible/outward-facing action class.

rules.text: Classify an action as irreversible/outward-facing by asking one question: does it change something a party outside my own local, uncommitted workspace can observe or depend on, or destroy data with no working restore path? A local commit is cheaply reversible (git-mastery §10 — reflog/fsck recovery); a git push, a tag, a package publish, a delete against a live datastore, or a deploy to a real environment is not, and belongs behind som-35.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was the irreversible/outward-facing classification made by checking whether the action is observable/consumable outside the local workspace or destroys unrecoverable data — not by a looser, unexamined judgment call?

rules.text: Surface a deprecation where its consumers will actually encounter it at the moment they use the deprecated path — a runtime warning, a compiler/linter deprecation diagnostic, or an in-code/doc-comment deprecation tag — not only in the changelog entry that lead-32 requires for the MINOR bump. A deprecation a consumer only learns about by reading changelogs before every upgrade is, in practice, a deprecation most consumers never see.

predicate.spec: a deprecated API surface emits a point-of-use signal (runtime warning, compiler/linter diagnostic, or equivalent) in addition to any changelog entry, so a consumer encounters the deprecation without having read release notes.

rules.text: A deprecation notice states three concrete facts, not merely the fact of deprecation itself: what to migrate to, by when (a concrete removal version or date, not 'eventually'), and — if a previously-deprecated path is later found actively unsafe rather than merely superseded — pair the notice with a visible Yanked-style marker (som-9) rather than a routine deprecation tag. [INFERRED — synthesis of the Yanked mechanic applied to the deprecation-severity case]

predicate.spec: a deprecation notice/warning names a migration target and a concrete removal version or date (not an open-ended 'eventually'), and an unsafe-superseded deprecation additionally carries a Yanked-style marker.

rules.text: Treat removal of a deprecated capability as a gated deletion, not a routine cleanup commit: it is a MAJOR-version change (the ownership call is lead-32/lead-33's job), and mechanically it gets the same irreversible-action confirmation as any other delete (som-35) — even though the deprecation itself was announced well in advance.

predicate.spec: the commit/PR that removes a previously-deprecated capability ships as a MAJOR version bump and passed through the som-35 explicit-authorization gate, rather than merging as an ordinary unreviewed cleanup.

rules.text: Wire a health-check/readiness endpoint, or an equivalent smoke test, directly into the deploy pipeline, run automatically immediately after a deploy completes, and gate 'deploy considered successful' on that check passing — a deploy that finishes without a pipeline error but was never smoke-tested is an unverified claim of health, the same failure shape as an unrestored backup (som-32). [INFERRED — standard deployment-verification practice]

predicate.spec: the deploy pipeline runs an automated health-check/smoke-test step immediately after deployment and the pipeline's success status depends on that step passing, not solely on the deploy command's own exit code.

rules.text: Route alerts on the signal that actually predicts user-visible harm — error rate, latency, saturation, the same class of postmortem trigger engineering-leadership §7 already defines (lead-44) — rather than on every anomaly a monitoring system can technically detect. An alert nobody acts on teaches the on-call rotation to ignore alerts, the same failure mode lead-20 describes for an unlabeled, default-mandatory review comment. [INFERRED — standard observability practice]

predicate.spec: configured alert rules are tied to user-visible-harm signals (error rate, latency, saturation, or an equivalent named postmortem trigger) rather than firing on every raw anomaly regardless of predictive value.

rules.text: Keep a runbook per incident class that names the exact rollback or mitigation command for that failure mode (tie directly to §5's rollback mechanics and §8's confirmation gate) — write it before the first real occurrence of that failure mode, not after, so the first occurrence is executed from a tested script rather than improvised under pressure. [INFERRED — standard incident-preparedness practice]

predicate.spec: each known incident class has a runbook document naming the concrete rollback/mitigation command(s) to run, authored/updated independent of whether that incident class has already occurred.

rules.text: This section covers only the mechanics around an incident — monitoring wiring, smoke gates, runbooks naming concrete rollback commands. The human process — blameless retrospectives, pre-defined postmortem triggers, and blame-free real-time incident communication — is engineering-leadership's job (§7 there, lead-44-lead-49); this module does not re-derive it, only the operational wiring that process runs on top of.
